utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You understand, Mr. Limaj, the affirmation still applies. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm going to take up where I left off last night and that is Rahovec. And to assist us, I am going to provide you with a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This map has been provided to Defence counsel and I'll also provided some copies for the Court. If it could be placed often the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, could you take a look at the map. I think it would be easier if you took at the actual map rather than on the screen.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you find Malisevo on that map? It's at the top.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then the road that runs to Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Here it is. Malisevo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter cannot hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you're following me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the interpreter is having trouble hearing you. That's the problem because you're not speaking into the microphone. Mr. Limaj, I understand, but on this map are you able to see the intersection where you outside of Rahovec where you say you went on -- at about 11.30 at night on the 17th of July? Are you able to see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you take a pen -- you may have one in your hand. Could you circle it, please?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are you able also to see -- find the village of Retimlje? Yeah, it's to the south -- yeah? Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please. I thought I saw it somewhere. It must be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention to the -- if you go down on the map it's sort of in the lower part of the map. Retimlje.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just circle that, please, the name?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is the one, but there used to be two Retimljes before, the upper and lower Retimlje. I don't know which one this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you look below the Retimlje you referred to there's a "D Retimlje" which perhaps refers to the lower. If you look at the Retimlje you've circled there's another Retimlje marked.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I circled writes [as interpreted] only Retimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Go lower --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other one has a "D" in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You can circle that one as well. And then do you see the village of Opterusa? Could you circle that as well, please.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you -- you can -- you don't need to look at the map any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- the -- but if it could be left there in case we need to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The place that you circled -- actually, just so the record is clear, I mean I think it probably is clear, but place you circled where you went, the inner section outside of Rahovec, could you just put a number 1 next to that. If you could just mark number 1 so it's clear which circle we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be clear, this is number 1 coming from Malisheve going to Rahovec but the one that goes round Rahovec. If you can see my finger here, this is the place where the road leads from Prizren to Rahovec. Maybe this will clear things up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I appreciate that clarification, but just so everything is very clear, the circle that you made with the number 1 next to it, that's the intersection where you went at 11.30 at night on the 17th of July; correct? Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From -- from 11.30 at night on the 17th until approximately 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning on the 19th when you fainted, were you at that location? Did you stay at that place?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I stayed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So can -- you arrive at 11.30 at night -- I don't think that was clear in your prior testimony, so if -- if we could clarify that now. You arrive at 11.30 at night at the place you marked 1, 11.30 at night on the 17th of July. When did you leave that location?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where did you go? Are you able to see on the map where you went?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you can see the road here, it's right about here. Probably it's closer to the bridge which was illustrated in the DVD that you showed, where the positions are for the protection of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just put a circle there where you're pointing and put a 2 just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if I understand you, then, at 11.30 at night on the 17th of July you arrived at the place where you've marked number 1. You spent some time -- that's where you found out about -- you say you found out about what was happening, at that place number 1? And then you proceeded to place number 2?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only two minutes, Mr. Prosecutor. I met two soldiers there. I asked them what was going on, and they told me that some soldiers from Malisheve has -- have gone to point number 2 that I marked here, number 2, and that's why I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where -- there were only two soldiers at point number 1?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, a couple, I said. Some. I don't know how many. There was confusion. There were many civilians. There were many civilians as well, so it was a confused situation. I can't tell you how many there were. It was total confusion. Nobody could tell you what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you -- then you proceeded to the point number 2 that you've marked, and did you remain at that place until you fainted on the morning of the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where I stayed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you -- in your testimony on direct examination when you were answering questions from Mr. Mansfield, you said that you -- when you were at that location you built up defence positions and you started digging trenches. Okay. Did you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you engage in any fighting? Did you actually have any encounters?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, there was no fighting, because -- I don't know if it's here in the map, but on that road, if you could see, this road here, this road leads to Prizren or Zerze. There is a village there, Bela Crkva, probably 10 or 12 kilometres away and there were units of the KLA there who fought against Serbian forces. That unit there, the following day. But we didn't fight in the place where we were. I personally did not fight, because I fainted before the Serbian forces came. I lost consciousness, so I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that on the -- the 18th you saw the representatives of the General Staff, Byslym Zyropi, Hashim Thaqi, Agim Qelaj. Jakup Krasniqi, was he...?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say Hashim Thaqi. I don't think I said that, because Hashim was not there. I think I said Sokol Bashota, Byslym and Agim Qelaj. And probably Muse Jashari. But it was very foggy for me at the time. I think these were the people that were present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, in response to a question from Mr. Topolski, you did say Hashim Thaqi. You said that Hashim Thaqi was also there. But are you now saying that he was not there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If I said that, maybe I made -- I made a mistake. But it was very hazy, as I said. The situation was such that I couldn't -- I can't remember. I fainted, as I said. But I don't think he was there. I don't think he was there. I know about Byslym and Agim because I was introduced to Agim, and somebody told me that he would become commander of that operation. There were people coming from all directions and he was in charge of coordinating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that it was very hazy then after you fainted, but is it hazy now, your memory of these events?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. It is hazy. You have to take everything I say about that period with some reservation because of the way I felt at the time, my health. I said this yesterday, and I said it before. Because of my health situation I'm not sure about what went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that, and I will take everything you say about that period with some reservation. Sitting here today, what is your best memory today, now, what is your best memory about whether you saw Hashim Thaqi? Do you think you did? Do you think you did? What's your best memory?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day -- I'm not sure about that day. I think it was the 20th or the 21st, if I'm not mistaken, that I saw him. On the 21st rather than the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But that would have been somewhere else. That's not in Rahovec then. That's in -- were you in Gajrak then or in Malisevo? Where --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not stay at Gajrak for a very long time. This was because the Serbian forces, after they took Rahovec, they started on their way to Malisheva. And, Your Honours, people were trying to protect -- to defend Malisheva because they thought because they had had this victory in Rahovec they would take Malisheva as well. So people were trying to defend Malisheva. Maybe we can illustrate this in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I do this on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In a moment that may be useful, but I'm just not clear. Were you involved -- were you in Malisevo on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say you think you saw Hashim Thaqi on the 21st. Where did you see him on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I saw him at one of these points on the road to Malisheve, because at that time they were trying to reinforce those points in order to defend Malisheva from the Serbian forces coming from Rahovec. There was fighting going on. The Serbs went towards Malisheve and that's why our forces were concentrated on the road to Malisevo in order to defend Malisevo, not to let the Serbian forces penetrate there. So the Serbian forces, after they took Rahovec, they started on the road to Malisevo but then they stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you -- did you go there and participate in trying to prevent the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was feeling sick. I went there to meet Sadik. Well, not to meet him but to learn about him, because I didn't know whether he was alive or dead. Everybody was looking for people at the time because many died at that time. Somebody told me that Sadik was alive, and he was there at the point where I went. And although I was very ill - I was with Sabit, I think - I went there. He was not there, so I returned because I was very ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can -- are you able to mark on the map where you went that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, when the Serbs took Rahovec, when it was completely under their control -- it was here, Mr. Prosecutor. So the Serbs had come here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that you had marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. On the 19th the Serbs had come at midday but I was at the hospital at the time so I don't know. But they had not stopped here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, this will go faster if you could just focus on the question. You talked about going on the 21st to a spot to look for Sadik or find information about Sadik. Are you able to mark on the map where that was that you went?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to explain the continuity of the Serb movements. That's why I did that. Mr. Prosecutor, I think it was somewhere about here. It's this line here that I drew. Is it okay if I draw a line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The line is fine. If you could put a 3 next to it.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, your testimony is as I understand it on the 21st you went to that spot.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think. But, Your Honours, as I said, I might make a mistake because the developments were such that I can make mistakes. The situation was totally confused. I think I went there to look for Sadik. There was a point here to stop the Serbs from going to Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long do you think you spent there? The best -- just your best memory.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten or 15 minutes, not more, I think. In fact, at the time when I was -- went there there was shelling and bullets as well, shelling from tanks. When we arrived there, the shelling started, so we went on the other side. We asked about him, and they told us that he was not there. So immediately I returned and continued with a therapy that I was receiving before, and then we heard about the information. I think it was on television that they announced that he had been killed, on the news. He had his ID in his pocket. That's how they had identified him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody had heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say it was announced on television, I take it you're talking about Albanian television, television from Albania.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The Serbian media as well. And our -- maybe our television referred to the Serbian media when they mentioned that. But it was -- the source was the Serbian media, because our television could not take that information without referring to the Serbs. The Serbs were there. We did not know anything. But he had his ID in his pocket, and that's how they identified him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Limaj, do I understand your testimony correctly that you think it was at this spot number 3 where you saw Hashim Thaqi on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where I think I saw him, because the members of the General Staff kept guard there because there was great risk to the population in that area. The population were trying to leave, to flee because of the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that were trying is to get to Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question was just about Hashim Thaqi. Aside from that occasion do you remember seeing him on any other occasion or was that the only occasion you remember seeing him? In connection with these events in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to speak the truth I can't tell you. It was very hazy at the time. It's still hazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I can't help you with this, but the situation was confused, as I said. And in addition to that, I was ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to point number 2 that you marked, and on the 18th you saw the representatives of the General Staff. Was -- I can't recall if you said -- did you say you saw Jakup Krasniqi? Was he one of them or no?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Adem Qelaj, Rexhep Selimi?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying no about Jakup Krasniqi because I think he was not at the positions. He never went to the positions. That's why I'm saying no. With regard to Rexhep Selimi, I think at the time he -- he was in Albania trying to get into Kosovo. I don't know whether he was in Albania, whether he had arrived in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he was trying to get into Kosovo. Byslym and Sokol I'm sure they were there and Agim Qelaj. You know why? Because it was at 6.00 in the morning or 7.00 in the morning when I went to point 1 where I went to ask people what was going on. There was such a great noise here and so many people. And I asked them, What's going on here? And the people were telling me nothing. We don't know anything. But these people have to be told where to go because there's such a big confusion here. But then the second time I can't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. You went at 6.00 or 7.00 in the morning of the 18th to position 1?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you saw the representatives of the General Staff at position 2; correct? Is that -- that's where you saw them on --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to position 2. I was referring to 1 where I saw them. I told you about that house where a kind of improvised and makeshift staff or headquarter were -- was established. On the DVD. We saw that on the DVD.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So now to be clear, from -- on the morning of the 18th you went back to position 1 and that's where you saw the representatives the General Staff. Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you saw them, did you return to position 2? Okay. Did you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see the representatives the General Staff again after that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the representatives of the staff, but Agim Qelaj, Agim Qelaj was left there. I don't know where the others went because Agim had the duty to coordinate everything. He came there to where I was staying and he gave instructions of about how to dig the trenches and reinforce the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was it the morning of the 19th that you saw -- you went back to position 1 and you saw Agim Qelaj there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went back to position 1 on the 19th in the morning, and then I fainted. But as I said, it's very confused in my mind what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at position 1 for the first time at 11.30 at night on the 17th, did any of the soldiers there tell you that a few hours before, at around 7.30 at night, they had stopped a man and his wife in a car with -- and their son and his wife and a child, a family of Serbs, that they had stopped them in their car? Did anyone tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They didn't tell you that they -- that they had separated the two older men and sent them to Malisevo and sent the rest of the family into Rahovec? You didn't hear anything about that when you were there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not at the time, no. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next when you returned to that position 1, did they tell you that the -- the women and the young grandson had driven -- had been taken through that position later that night after you left, at about 1.00 in the morning, and taken to Malisevo right through that spot number 1? Did anyone tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. There were 500 or 600 people there minimum coming from various places. Armed. There were 5 or 6.000 civilians trying to flee. There were people coming in and going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm talking about Serb civilians who were stopped and detained. I'm just trying to find out if you heard anything about this.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you, but I'm trying to explain how the situation was. It was impossible. There were hundreds of people there. Many people were saying various things, and they didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But did you hear anything about it? Did anyone tell you anything about it? Did you hear anything about --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- about Serb civilians being taken prisoner and being taken to Malisevo from Rahovec? Did you hear anything on --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the 18th did you hear anything about the KLA -- well, it's starting the night of the 17th and going into the morning of the 18th that the Serbs attacked houses in Opterusa. Did anybody tell you anything about that? The representatives of the General Staff or the soldiers did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just answer the question, please. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to tell you what I heard. Yes, I will. The units, various units, I heard that fighting started in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Limaj. I'm just going to interrupt you because the interpreter was not able to hear. You said you heard fighting started in, and the interpreter could not hear the name of the village. So if you could just start over with your answer. You heard that fighting started --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that fighting started from Suhareke, from the bases in Suhareke to the bases in Opterushe, towards Rahovec. I don't know where Opterushe is, but I know to -- to go to Suhareke you have to pash from Opterushe. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the story that you gave to the Court in your direct examination about how the fighting in Rahovec started was that there was -- there were -- there were shots fired in the -- in the town of Rahovec and units that were stationed around Rahovec were concerned and everybody spontaneously rushed into the town. Can you explain how, then, this fighting occurred on the night of the 17th, morning of the 18th in Opterusa, which is quite -- as you can see on the map quite a bit aways from Rahovec. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. On the 17th or 18th -- I think it was on the 18th that the great confusion was. When the fighting started in Rahovec they left from Suha Reka to help in that area. I think this is how the fighting must have started. This is the logic of it. I'm just supposing this was so because I don't know. That is another part. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, isn't it a fact -- in fact, this was an organised attack by the KLA on Rahovec and the villages surrounding Rahovec? This was an organised and planned attack.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know what you you're saying now. I can't tell the difference between organised and unorganised. I don't know, then, in this world what you can refer to as unorganised. From the very beginning during the war, after the war, everyone who has referred to the Rahovec case has told the truth. That was total confusion. Civilians took part in fighting. Soldiers took part in fighting. People came from various places. Nobody can tell what happened. It was not organised, or at least I think so. I gave you my example. Mr. Prosecutor, nothing was organised there. Every observer who was there could testify to that because if that was organised, there were 3 or 400 special police forces involved. There was -- it was not organised. It was a total confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, did you also hear on the morning of the 18th there was Serb houses in the village of Retimlje were attacked? Did you hear anything about that? And that some 16 Serb men were taken from Retimlje and have never been seen alive again? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that there were fighting all over, but about the village you are asking me, I can't tell you specifically about that. I referred to Bela Crkva. Fighting here, fighting there, fighting outside, all over. We didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you still maintain that this was spontaneous. There was fighting everywhere and you still maintain it was spontaneous. Everybody started fighting at the same time. That's your position, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir. I told you how things started. This was like a chain, you know, one started here and then the other said, "Let's go and help. What is happening in Rahovec?" This is how it started. There were Serb positions. The Serbs prevented them, so they had to fight with the Serbs. This is how it happened. If it started as you are saying, Mr. Prosecutor, then they should have organised the fighting very well in Bela Crkva and not have 10 or 15 soldiers killed there of ours who were coming to help in Rahovec. Hundreds and thousands of people were there and nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In those days following the fighting in Rahovec, did you ever hear about Serb civilians, men who had been taken from Opterusa, Retimlje and from Rahovec itself being held prisoner in Malisevo for a period of about ten days? Did you hear about that happening?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. To tell you the truth, the main concern for us that -- my -- my personal concern at that time was the murder of those fighters and the confused situation. So I was not focused on that event. As I told you, people were talking about what happened in Rahovec. They were saying that the Serbs were violating women and perpetrating all sorts of crimes. Many soldiers were lost. Nobody knew where they were. Not at that time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the moment I'm trying -- Mr. Limaj, at the moment I'm trying to focus on these Serb civilians that were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just focus on them, please. Did you hear anything about a plan to take civilians prisoner in order to exchange them for KLA soldiers who had been taken prisoner by the Serbs? Did you hear -- in your meetings with the General Staff or the representatives of the General Staff, did you ever hear anything about such a plan to take prisoner that would be used as an exchange?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you hear that some KLA soldiers were taken about the Serbs, you are saying? This is the first time for me to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. My question maybe was unclear. Did you ever hear about a plan to take Serb civilians prisoner in order to exchange them for KLA soldiers or Albanians who had been taken prisoner by the Serbs? Did you -- just yes or no. Did you ever hear about such a plan?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time for me to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you ever hear about prisoner who were being held in Malisevo or elsewhere later being executed by the KLA? No? You're shaking your head no.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might. The number of questions that have been asked over this last period of time, and I do appreciate the fact that this is cross-examination and a wide latitude has been given and should be given in cross-examination, but questions that say "Did you ever hear" without any attributions whatsoever to any authors of this information are so far-reaching that the extent to which at any point anyone would rely - whether or not the answer is affirmative or negative and it has been consistently negative - but that anyone would rely on any of these questions having any basis in fact I think is something that is important to note solely for purpose of the record. Because it is rank hearsay of the worst kind, without any attribution as to time, place, or author. And I rise solely for purpose of objecting for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. If there had been a positive response, I would expect there to have been a more detailed follow-up if it was considered that any weight should be attached to the matter as all. But as you've indicated, there have been negative responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Limaj, I just want to go back to the documentary that was made about Sadik Shala who died in Rahovec. Before I do, you obviously participated in the making of that documentary; right? I mean, you're shown in the documentary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers pause between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't take part in it. I had to wait a long time before I was able to make that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, we've been asked by the interpreters to pause between question and answer, so after I ask a question if you can pause for a pause before answering and I'll try to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe my question is unclear. You were interviewed for that documentary and in fact you appear speaking during the documentary for Sadik Shala; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I speak about his life, this is all. I made a statement only on his life. I don't know what you think. I gave that statement. On the occasion of that event. I said what I knew, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, after the documentary was broadcast on television, did you ever make any complaints that the documentary about your nephew's life was inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make any complaints, but I told the reporters immediately. I didn't see it direct on the spot. I saw it afterwards in the video cassette. I saw that there were mistakes there, that they had not described the situation as it really was. Mr. Prosecutor, when you spoke for a documentary, you just sum up events. You cannot go into details. And sometimes it happens that you may not speak in detail or exactly about things, just summing up of the events. I know that there were -- that there are some mistakes. They are not major mistakes. I think they are mistakes that can be improved if you write a book. But usually if you look at all documentary programmes made on martyrs in Kosova, there are always such mistakes because you look at events from a different perspective, not from what happened in the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you said you told the reporters immediately. Do you know the reporters by name that you told?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nuhi Bytyci. He was the author of that documentary. I said this is not entirely so. I even told him that I too was incapable of improving it at that moment. But he insisted that I give my version of the story and I said what I thought at that moment. But just speaking in general, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to play a short clip from that documentary and give you an opportunity to comment on it. This is from Prosecution Exhibit P34. And if we could switch to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to hear that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just have a couple questions about that. First of all, it describes the KLA soldiers as being fired with enthusiasm for liberating the town. That's in fact what was happening. The KLA -- there was an effort to take the town by the KLA, take control of that town. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was waiting for the interpreter to finish. I have a tooth pain. I'm sorry, I apologise. I had a pain all night and so I have to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just -- just -- are you able to -- are you able to continue? Are you able to focus?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you have any difficulty because of the tooth pain concentrating, it's important that you tell us. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the moment I can, but I was sleepless all night because of the tooth pain. With respect to what we saw here in this newsreel, Mr. Prosecutor, this is a recording made by EuroNews. It is not filmed by Albanian television crews, as far as I know. This is made for the media, Mr. Prosecutor. You cannot rely on that. I'm telling you again that the Serb forces never moved from Rahovec. That is the truth. You have documents you yourself have provided here that hundreds of policemen, Serb policemen, were stationed there. Before -- four days before events in Rahovec, if I am not wrong, there were Serbian special intervention forces deployed there. They were there permanently, all the time. It is true that -- that our forces took hold of 70 or 80 per cent of Rahovec, but we never took it completely. It was a confusion. It rained for one and a half days. That is the reality of Rahovec as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the other --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have said -- we have declared that that's a fact that we took Rahovec, in the media. That's what we declared that's true. 90 per cent of the territory is under our control, we have declared that, but I think that was only for the media. That doesn't coincide with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The other question I had about this clip was that there's a reference to "Celiku's soldiers of the 121 Brigade." Now, isn't it a fact, Mr. Limaj, that in everything but name the 121 Brigade existed at the time of Rahovec? It didn't have the name but otherwise in everything but name the 121 Brigade existed that's why there is a reference to "Celiku's soldiers of the 121 Brigade" fighting in Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were units from various units, Mr. Prosecutor. Sadik was a member of the Celiku unit. You -- some said Celiku 1, Celiku 2, but he was, that's a fact. The reporter mentions Brigade 121 because you knew Sadik was a member of the Celiku unit, but that didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was -- I'm pausing. Was there a plan in -- according to you to create the 121 Brigade before the offensive, Serb offensive, at the end of July? In other words, was there -- did the plan exist before the offensive?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of June, the beginning of July, if I am not mistake - I don't want to repeat what we have already discussed together - after developments in Malisheve it became immediate for us to appoint the commanders of Pashtrik and Nerodimlje zones. This was something that the General Staff thought we should do immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt you to try to move things along here. Can you focus on the 121 Brigade. You're talking about the Pashtrik zone, the Nerodimlje zone. Focus on the 121st Brigade. The question is was there a plan according to you to create the 121 Brigade after the offensive at the end of July or was that plan only devised after the offensive?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I tried to explain to you that we couldn't form brigades before dividing the zones. With respect to Brigade 121st, I have never heard about that. I never heard how the brigades would be formed and called. I didn't hear about any numbers. After August, I started to hear first about Brigade 121, 61, 68, 122nd and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But before that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just to be clear, you did not hear about any plan -- don't focus on the name. You did not hear about any plan to form the brigade until August. That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not letting me to explain. The plan was when the zone commander was appointed, the plan was to build the zone and to divide into brigades. That was a plan in July. But first you had to divide the zones, then start talks with the units to form brigades to see what territory each brigade would cover and so on. That was meant to be. But we didn't know how they would call the brigades and what place they would cover because we couldn't finish. We couldn't realise the plan. The Pashtrik zone remained only with one commander without any other structure. He didn't have even a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So even according to you the planning of creating this brigade, which later was called the 121 Brigade, the planning started in July?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the plan for a brigade but in July -- July this is what happened: The zone commander was appointed, a commander of Nerodimlje and Pashtrik. Then we said after appointing the commander we should form the zones and begin talks with the units to start the restructuring of the KLA. That commander waited for directives from the General Staff as to what to do, how many brigades to form, where to form the brigades, how to call them. All these things were interrupted during the offensive, so we couldn't talk about the places, the number, or the territories. Only the zone commander was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play another clip and this is from the interview. It's from P36. This is an interview with you so these are your own words. It's clip number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, there in that account you say that you were together with Hashim Thaqi during the fighting and you took turns on duty. That's quite different what you -- than what you've told this Court today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's not different. I said that the members of the General Staff took turns to do their duty. It's just a summary of what happened. This is a fact, what I'm saying. I told you that they took turns. Among them was Hashim. I went there for a couple of minutes to see how the situation was. I was in Rahovec on the 17th. He might have been somewhere else. We may have met there. This is what I meant. Hashim was not with me on the front lines. This is a summary of developments. You may take it out of context and interpret it as you wish, but this is the truth. I think this is summary of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see I say a commander of Brigade 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you knew that was going to be my next question. But before I ask that question, your testimony is that what you said in that little clip that we just saw and what you've said in court today is the same, is consistent? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am explaining to you. That is just a summary. It's not the same thing to talk -- to testify before the court and make a description for the media. In general --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Mr. Limaj, but when we started off the cross-examination, you told me in the most emphatic terms that you -- nobody was more truthful or transparent with the media than you. Now are you saying that when you speak to the media you can be inaccurate? Are you changing your testimony now about your telling the truth to the media?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it is a fact that I was in Rahovec and I told the media a truth. I am telling a truth here too. The only difference is that I didn't go into details as I am doing here. I told the media I was in Rahovec, that we were on duty, we took turns. I spoke in general. I didn't speak personally. I meant the General Staff. I was there for three days. I didn't say I was there all the time. I couldn't be there every minute of the day, but I was there. I didn't lie to the media about anything and I'm not lying here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, do you have different truths for different places?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. That is what you are saying. That is not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You have one truth when you're speaking in Kosovo and the media and you have another truth when you come here to the courtroom? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. My testimony is the same from the beginning to now. There is no other truth. Please don't try to distort things from the summary of a documentary which in general proves what I'm saying here. There may be differences or gaps, but I didn't go into any details. I didn't say to them that I was injured, that I had that faint fit. There are things which I didn't tell them. I just summed up some developments. They asked me -- I explained how the General Staff stayed close to the soldiers, that we went on duty there and that Brigade 121st knows. Everybody knows when it was formed. I didn't mean to lie there. If you talk about units then it doesn't make sense. So people got used to hearing the mention of brigade 121st. I couldn't speak about all the units that formed it. What could I say? There were -- there was nothing before that time. You can interpreter it as you wish, but this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, let's move forward. I'm going to ask you be shown Prosecution Exhibit P44, which is an article dated the 3rd of September, 1998, in Zeri i Kosoves. Do you recall this interview with Zeri i Kosoves, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I gave it but I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could turn to the second page in Albanian and in English it's on the second page closer to the top. Do you see the question from the newspaper, "This fire of war burned the enemies in the straight of Lapusnik where you were in command and it was personified in the straight of Kacanik?" And then your response is, "There was combat and resistance there that own the Albanians know how to carry out." Do you see that? "With the assistance of other units that were positioned on the other side of the straight, the Pellumbi and Guri units and of course with the sacrifice and fighting spirit of our three units we dealt a strong blow to the enemy." Now, that's a reference to the 9th of May battle; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been about the 9th of May or it might have been about other battles because there were other battles waged in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the two big battles that you dealt a strong blow to the enemy were the 9th of May and the 29th of May. So is it a reference to one of those two battles?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were battles. There was another battle on the 25th as well. I think it refers to battles in general, the battles waged in Lapusnik without singling out any specific battle. It talks about fighting, think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's your words, so I'm just asking you what --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you think what you're referring to is the battles in general from May to July 1998 in Lapusnik. That's what you think you're referring to there.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look carefully, we can see that -- he's reading again what you just read before, the same words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you have to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just repeated what you said. I think that it talks about the end more than the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So now you think that this is a reference to the battles at the end in July of 1998. Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be the battle of the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: 29th of which month?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of May. Second battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that would make sense, wouldn't it, because the -- that's a battle -- certainly the 9th of May and the 29th of May of 1998 were battles where you dealt a strong blow to the enemy. So it would --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th battle was also a major battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: People fought. It was a battle. Yeah, it may refer to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, these are your words. What's your best memory of what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this refers to fighting in Lapusnik, to fighting in general. And it mentions two units, Guri, Pellumbi and our three units, Celiku 1, 2 and 3, units that participated in fighting there. This is what I have stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear, these are your words; correct? This is what you said?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We're done with that. Mr. Limaj, I want to go back to something that we talked about at the beginning, and that is about getting international support for the KLA, that the KLA certainly in 1998 was -- one of its goals was to get support from the international community, and I believe that I asked you that at the beginning and that's something you accepted at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in the transcript I see a minor mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's the mistake that you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say here Guri, Pellumbi and the three -- our three one its, 1, 2 and 3, that is Celiku units, they are part of Brigade 121st, and I mentioned these three units that participated in the battle of Lapusnik or in fightings -- fighting in Lapusnik. Because a person who later became a commander of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the -- I'm a little unclear now what you've just said. The Guri and Pellumbi units were on the other side of the asphalt road; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about our three units because this interview -- I gave this interview as commander of the Brigade 121st. I'm telling here that the three units were fighting there. This is the meaning of it. This is what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, going back to the -- what I was moving on to. You recall testifying that one of the goals of the KLA during 1998 was to get support from the international community?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as parts of that effort the KLA wanted to show the international community that it was following the rules of warfare while the Serbs were not; correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot add anything to Jakup Krasniqi's comments. This is politics, and Jakup Krasniqi dealt with such matters at the time. He was a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He was in fact what he said in this courtroom and perhaps this is what you're referring to when you say you can't add anything to his comments, he said, "We had frequent contacts with the representatives of the international community, and because we respected the international documents on citizens, we were supported by the internationality community." Now, you agree with that, right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. The aim of the KLA was to be behave within that behaviour that is acceptable for the international community, and this is one of the conditions for its aspirations to become true. This was an orientation and a constant strive of the KLA towards this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I noticed just a moment ago that you held the side of your mouth again. I just want to remind you that if you're having any difficulty because of the pain in your mouth concentrating on my questions, any difficulty at all with this, I don't think there would be any problem with taking a break or interrupting. It's very important that you're able to focus on concentrate on these questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to continue? Do you have any difficulty at all?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please, if you have any difficulty, it's very important that you say something. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that in June of 1998 you -- as I understand your testimony, you received a rule book.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could Mr. Limaj be shown Prosecution Exhibit P156, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was, to my recollection, on the 22nd or 23rd of June when I received the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, before you is Prosecution Exhibit P156. Is this the same book that you received?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you read this book?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I notice that your name is in fact used -- your pseudonym is in fact used as an example, used as an example in the book. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. My pseudonym was not taken as an example. Please. This was compiled in Albania, this rule book. The name Celiku mentioned here is just a coincidence, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Ramadan Behluli testified that when he joined as a soldier, when he joined the KLA on the 20th of April, 1998, he was told certain rules by Luan, Ramiz Qeriqi, and some of the rules he was told was do not use -- do not misuse the uniform for personal reasons, acts of revenge are forbidden, and that in the case of violations soldiers would be held responsible. And he was also told some rules, though he couldn't recall them specifically, about the treatment of civilians. Do you recall at that time, in April of 1998, that those rules were -- even before this book -- even before you saw this book that those sorts of rules were generally shared and communicated among the KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, with full responsibility I tell you that there wasn't any rule book or a document in the hands of KLA soldiers before this document came on the 22nd of June. And even when I received it on the 22nd of June, Jakup Krasniqi told me that he only had five copies of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt you because I don't think -- you either didn't listen or you didn't understand my question, and I appreciate it was a long question, but my question was -- put aside the book for a moment. Go back to April of 1998. Even before the book was in existence, KLA -- there was talk among soldiers about rules such as do not misuse the uniform, do not engage in acts of personal revenge, and that if there were violations soldiers would be held responsible, and rules about treatment of civilians. Those kinds of rules were discussed orally even by April of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What people discussed amongst themselves as soldier to soldier, a civilian to soldier, this is quite a different issue. Such conversations could have occurred between everybody. I even myself spoke about civilians and soldiers at that time. But as a rule, as something determined by the KLA, this did not exist. People could speak of their own visions, how they perceived this issue. I have many times referred to those communiques when I spoke of the KLA with the public, because in order to speak to the citizens what should be done to raise money and things like that you had to refer to some source. But as I said, we didn't have anything concrete, in writing, any rule in writing before the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But even by April and May of 1998, you say that you spoke with civilians and soldiers about such matters, about respecting the rules and about the rules of warfare and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already told you how it was in April and May, what the reality was at that time, at the time those four or five soldiers that we were. We discussed this, but later on when we removed the mass of people from there we did sit down and present our vision, how we will continue, but this all happened later on. In April and May we were only four or five. There was nothing to discuss about. But later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But just to go back to Ramadan Behluli, he testified in this courtroom that in April of 1998 he joins the KLA as an ordinary soldier, that he heard about -- that he was told these rules. You heard about such rules at that time as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no rules, Mr. Prosecutor. When you asked him about the oath, whether he took oath, he said, "Yes, I did it on my own in front of the flag." So this shows that everyone could do whatever they wanted. There were no such rules. I'm telling you that these rules did not exist at that time. And you know that, but what you're trying to say is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just putting to you what Ramadan Behluli said in this courtroom about rules that he heard in April of 1998. You're telling us that you didn't -- you didn't have any discussions or hear anything about such rules at that time. Is that your testimony? In April of 1998 or May of 1998.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such rule. Even when you asked Ramadan Behluli to repeat what he had said then, he was not able to do that because he did not remember the words. If there were such rules, Mr. Krasniqi would have mentioned that. What people did individually, I don't know that. Someone was speaking about Kosovo, someone from Macedonia, and -- but they were all their own views.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is a convenient time. Or would you like me to press on? It's -- it's almost an hour and a half, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It's not quite yet, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I'm about to enter a topic that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: An entirely new topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, because we've had a break I'm just going to remind you again that if you have any difficulty at all continuing, just please say so because of the pain in your mouth or for any other reason. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your concern. Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move now to a meeting that you had with Jan Kickert, Jakup Krasniqi, David Slinn on the 30th of July in Klecke. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Ram Buja was also there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At that time, Ram Buja had the responsibility for organising civil authorities in the free area around Malisevo and -- the free areas controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What according to you was his duty at that time or in the weeks leading up to that time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will now tell you what I was told at that time. Your Honours, he was the political counter of Mr. Krasniqi at that time. I knew Ram Buja because we became members of the General Staff together. Myself, Ram Buja and Adem Grabovci were appointed members of the General Staff at the same time. He was at that time a counsellor. Whether he worked in the organisation of civil authorities at that time while he was a consultant, I don't know, but I think that he became the person in charge for organising civil authorities sometime in December. At the time you are referring to, he was only a counsellor. This is what he said he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall during that meeting Jakup Krasniqi stating, telling the international representatives Jan Kickert and David Slinn that the KLA recognised its responsibilities under international law? Do you recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this was a political topic that was discussed since the offensive was still ongoing. On one hand the offensive was discussed and on the other side the political activities, the attempts of the European Union to create a joint government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, maybe you didn't -- you either didn't listen or you didn't understand my question. My question is did Jakup Krasniqi -- do you recall Jakup Krasniqi saying that the KLA recognised its responsibilities under international law?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jakup Krasniqi said that in this meeting the KLA will respect the international conventions about the war and this was the attempt to present the KLA in the best light before the international factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to your meeting in November of 1998 with Human Rights Watch. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me personally, this was the first official meeting, because on the 31st, they were in my base. I was there when they came, and I consider it my first meeting with international officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say on the 31st. The 31st of which month?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking of the 31st July, about the meeting we just discussed with Jan Kickert and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. I'm moving on to a different meeting now, okay?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, to November of 1998 when you met -- you and Hashim Thaqi met with Peter Bouckaert and Fred Abrahams of Human Rights Watch. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this was held in my birthplace in Banje village. I don't know who arranged it but I know that I was called for this meeting. They came up to a place near Banje and then soldiers escorted them and I found a place where to meet in Banje. But I don't know how the meeting was arranged to be held in Banje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall being introduced at the meeting as the head of the legal department of the general headquarters of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this, but this is a misunderstanding because this was never the case in my life. The General Staff never had such a department. I don't know how it came to -- how it happened for this misunderstanding to take place. They were meeting in my territory. I was presented before them as Commander Celiku. We sat down. The discussion began. And I wasn't introduced in the capacity of what you said. And as I said, as it was no such department, logically I could not have been presented as such. I was presented as a person who had a legal background, but this could have been the misunderstanding, but as I said, I introduced myself as Commander Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why were you presented as a person with a legal background?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a legal background. That was the first meeting. We introduced ourselves. "What is your profession? What have you completed in the past?" This was informal discussion just to get to know each other. The journalist who was accompanying them, we used to be -- to study together in the past, and he told them I was doing a post-graduate study just to introduce me. I just introduced personally myself as Commander Celiku, not as commander of the 121 Brigade. I don't know how they interpreted this, but as I said, such a department did not exist within the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Regardless of whether the department existed or not, in fact you're certain that you were not introduced as being the head of the legal department of the general headquarters. That's your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This absolutely does not stand. As I said, it must be a misunderstanding. There was no one to introduce me and neither I myself introduced myself as such. From my background, maybe during that informal talk in the beginning of the meeting they understood me to be such, but myself, I introduced myself as Commander Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The meeting was about two Serb journalists who had been stopped and detained by the KLA; correct? Two journalists from Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a case, a reason, but it was obvious that the two gentlemen from this well-known institution wanted to meet us even earlier. This was one of the reasons, but they felt it necessary to meet KLA members for other issues as well. They wanted to establish the first contact with the KLA because until then there wasn't such a contact between them and the KLA. But as a very important issue to be treated on that meeting for them was the issue of the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you ended up at that meeting simply because the meeting was held in Banje? That's the only reason that you were there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the only reason, because the meeting was held in the territory of my brigade. I accompanied Mr. Thaqi. There was no one else to accompany him. And I even didn't know who we were meeting. It's when I entered inside the room that I realised who we were meeting. So since this meeting occurred in my zone, into my birthplace in Banje, it was organised in an oda, a guest room. We had this informal talk before the meeting and then we treated the issues that interested them. This was how it happened, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you participated in the meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We discussed. It was an informal meeting, as I said, and we treated different issues. We were three or four. We exchanged views. I spoke there as well, of course less that others. It was Mr. Thaqi who was speaking, but I did join the discussion when there was a subject brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, let's talk specifically about the two journalists. You told the representatives of Human Rights Watch that the two journalists had been tried and convicted; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was. It was a General Staff communique. I don't know whether I said that or Mr. Hashim Thaqi, but that's how it was. They were aware of that. It was a public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told the representatives of Human Rights Watch that the two journalists had not about present at their trial where they were tried and convicted; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was or should be. I don't remember anything specific, but this is how it should be. There was some notes taken. I don't remember everything that was said, every word that was uttered during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, do you remember saying those words? Do you remember saying those words or somebody else saying those words, that the journalists were not present at their trial?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- did you think that was a proper trial?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was an improvised trial, Mr. Prosecutor. There was no trial. Later on when we realised -- when they entered, we realised that it was an improvised trial. Later on when I joined the General Staff, I realised it was an improvised trial and there was no trial at all. It was an improvised trial just for the sake of the media. They released a communique and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There was no trial, in fact, was there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no trial. As I said, when I joined in December, I saw that there was no trial. Simply it was a propaganda, an improvised trial. I don't know how to label it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference between no trial and an improvised trial. Those are two very different things. You appreciate the difference; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, but what I meant was different. "Improvised" here is in a meaning that they wanted to say that they had kind of a trial. I don't know how clear I was on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I understand you. Let me see if I understand you. There was no trial, but they said there was a trial. The KLA said there was a trial.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The KLA said in its communique that there were -- there was a trial and that these journalists have been convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in fact the truth is that these journalists were held without a trial; right? There was no trial.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be held is something different. They were held without trial, but to be detained is something different, and we can discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm very interested to know what the difference is between being held and being detained, and I'm -- maybe you can also share with us why you find it funny.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the way I expressed myself was not quite the right way, but what I meant was when they were stopped, the journalists, while passing in our territory, this is what I meant by being held. This was my mistake, and that's why I laughed a little bit. I'm sorry for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's try to be absolutely clear because these are very important matters. These journalists were stopped and they were detained; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They were detained by the KLA. They were not given a trial.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told Human Rights Watch that they had been given a trial.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we referred to that communique. Mr. Thaqi referred to the General Staff communique, Your Honours. Personally, I wasn't a member of the General Staff, and I didn't know whether there was or there wasn't a trial. They simply referred to that public communique that they were convicted after the military trial. But as I said, when I joined the General Staff in December, I realised that there wasn't such a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The members of Human Rights Watch asked for access to the two journalists who were then being held as prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It should be like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you denied them access to the prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, that was the first meeting. We had our reserves. We didn't know whether the General Staff was going to approve that or not. At least this is how I saw Mr. Thaqi. Personally, I didn't have any role in that. Mr. Thaqi had not discussed that with the General Staff, and we left that to be treated in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, to be clear, Mr. Thaqi was on the General Staff at that time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time Mr. Thaqi was a political representative, a public figure, but he was, as I said, a political representative, not a military representative of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when Human Rights Watch asked to have access to the prisoners, you didn't say, "We need to consult with the General Staff on this matter," you said, "No, you may not have access to the prisoners"; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, Mr. Thaqi told them that, "For the moment you cannot do that." They were supposed to be released, and I think he told them we should consult the military wing. This is what I remember him telling them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You recall Mr. Thaqi saying that they were going to be released?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that we will do our best to release them. It was a friendly talk. We were -- he said that, "We will do our best to fulfil your request, the release." The entire conversation was directed in finding the most suitable form. We told them that we were ready to cooperate, and this was the meaning of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Limaj, didn't you say that this was a matter for the judicial authorities and you did not want to interfere with the independence of the judicial authorities? Isn't that in fact what you said?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We said it was a military issue. I don't remember quite clearly it now, but I think that we said it was a military issue. I don't know how court-martial was realised at that time, but to my knowledge, what was said was -- Mr. Thaqi said that we cannot do anything about it for the moment because the military wing is going to consult it, but we will do our best to fulfil your request. This is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's your memory of what he said?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately. I am saying again this is the approximate version of the meeting. The meeting had one purpose, to find a solution. There might be differences here and there, but this was the essence of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in your answers you keep saying that "Mr. Thaqi said," "Mr. Thaqi said" with respect to these issues of the prisoners. Didn't you in fact talk about these two prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course we did talk about these prisoners. We said that they entered the KLA territory, that we suspected them of being Serb spies and that they did not respect a decision that was brought by the General Staff which was to get a permission to enter the territory controlled by the KLA.
