I also said that they were in good health, that they're being treated well. This is what was discussed. And in a way, we explained why they were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you know that they were in good health and being treated well? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were detained in the territory of my brigade, and I had gone to visit them, Your Honours, and I knew that they were in good health. And they remained in good health until the very end. They were treated very well, to the means that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were they detained specifically?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were stopped at Resinovc, as I recollect. Your Honours, maybe I can describe this on the map as well. Where Magure is, at that time in November Magure was the boundary between the KLA and the Serb forces. Behind Magure there are some Albanian villages and little bit more below is the village of Resinovc. There was a unit of mine there that was positioned there in that village. The two journalists -- do you want me to explain how they were stopped? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question was where they were held. What village were they held in?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were held in Resinovc. When I visited them it was in Resinovc. My deputy commander, he was there when they were detained, and I instructed him to look after them properly until their very release. The day when they were stopped, my deputy was visiting, paying a visit to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went to visit them, where specifically in Resinovc were they being held? Can you describe it? Was it a house? Was it a building? What?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were detained in a school building. It was a small school building, in a classroom. And from there, my deputy, whose name is Shaban Draga, I instructed him to take care of them. I was not there all the time, but he was informing me and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the place where they were detained in the school building, in the classroom, were they -- were there other prisoners or were they detained alone?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is just a -- of someone being detained by chance. They entered our zone. The soldiers stopped them, checked them. They found documents. They saw Mr. Milosevic's photograph. This is the main reason. They saw the membership card of SPS, and they were questioned. One of them was very stubborn and was persisting in entering his own territory. And when he was asked whether he had the permission from Demaqi to enter KLA territory, he said that, "I don't need such a permission. I can walk freely in my territory, in my country." I immediately reported this to the General Staff, and I think that I immediately, the following day, went to visit them. I had a coffee with them. And he said openly that he was a Tanjug journalist, he supports Milosevic's policy, "But I'm not a spy. I just entered your territory to film the area and to complete my duty as a journalist." Because of course we had our suspicions because the General Staff wanted us to investigate. They probably checked it through Pristina whether they were really journalists or not. And then the General Staff did what it did, the detention, and they came out with a communique, and then this conviction and trial was mentioned. So the reason why they were there is they broke the rule. They entered the territory without Adem Demaqi's permission. This is the reason why they were held that long. There was no other reason the they were not what we suspected. They were not spies. The only reason was they broke the rules. They did not respect the rules. They didn't go to Demaqi for permission, and that's why then their release was negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, how long were they held?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, they were held, if I'm not mistaken, for around a month and a half, approximately. I don't know the exact date when they were arrested, but I know that they were released before the November holidays. The General Staff then, in the name of the holiday, pardoned them, and this was all just to show the world that something is allegedly functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to the meeting. The representatives of Human Rights Watch also asked for the KLA's code of conduct. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you remember refusing to provide it to the Human Rights Watch? Do you remember Mr. Thaqi --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- also saying that there had been disciplinary proceedings against some KLA members? Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi said something else. He didn't say exactly how you're putting it. He said we were -- "We are trying to build up a discipline, a rule." But as for this code of conduct, there was nothing to offer. It was a disgrace. We were telling them that such a code of conduct was being prepared in Tirana. We told them that we have such problems but we're doing our best to fix them. We do have information that in certain points KLA soldiers are behaving badly. These were the subjects that were discussed. As what you mentioned as code of conduct, he referred to this book of rules. And it was under refusal, actually. We told him we would send that in the future. I remembered that he said clearly he would bring the code of conduct in the next meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that -- you said, and I'm reading from the monitor here, you said, "We told them that we have such problems but we're doing our best to fix them. We do have information that in certain points KLA soldiers are behaving badly." What were you referring to when you said that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi was referring to the developments after September. There was a kind of discontinuity because the offensive had destroyed us in a way, so we were trying to reconstruct what we had. There were such things at that time in the beginning when the brigades were formed because people had deserted. They had left. Many -- some people had done things in the name of the KLA although they were in civilian clothes. People, after August, had left the army and had gone on to do business. So there was a tendency, a trend. We were trying to work and improve our work. But there was nothing that was specified in this direction. At least I can't remember that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I've just going to pursue this a little further because the words you used were "in certain points KLA soldiers are behaving badly." Now, when you explained that you said there were soldiers there were people who left the KLA and were behaving badly. Is that what you were referring to when you said "KLA soldiers are behaving badly" or were you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I was clear in what I said. With this new organisation that we were trying to do, there would be more opportunity for us with this new organisation to see the mistakes or misbehaviours of the soldiers. We spoke about things in general, but we did not specify any cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand you did not specify any cases, but did you have any specific cases in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honours, this was not the same as the situation in August, up to August. Until August, somebody could come to the army, stay for a week in the army and go back to his family, stay for a week with his family or do business somewhere, sell arms or weapons somewhere. So there were cases of soldiers who left the army after they had committed to become soldiers in the army. And at that time, it was important for us to know who our soldiers were. We needed to know that we had certain number of soldiers who would be ready to fight. Sometimes it happened that we thought we had 5 or 600 soldiers and then in the end we ended up with only 20 when we were facing the Serb forces. So that's why we wanted to have some rules and have the number of soldiers, who these soldiers are in order to control the situation. We discussed this at length, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move to a different topic, Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I would like to emphasise one thing. Your Honours, about these two journalists, after the meeting with Human Rights Watch - I can't pronounce their name - I invited them -- I invited the Red Cross through the General Staff. The Red Cross came and visited them. Their families communicated with them. Clothes were brought to them and food was brought to them, so they had the opportunity to communicate with their families. Once or twice they brought clothes and they communicated by writing, by letters. But I wanted to emphasise the Red Cross visited these two people after the meeting. The deputy commander, my deputy commander accompanied them during their visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand and appreciate that information. That was all after the meeting with Human Rights Watch; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I think it was after that, but you can confirm that with the Red Cross. What is for sure is that the Red Cross has come to visit them, brought them letters from their families. My deputy also offered them medical help because there was a doctor nearby. And both of them were fair to us. They described their detention the way it was, the way they were treated. They did not say anything bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, speaking of the Red Cross, Jakup Krasniqi testified in court here that the Red Cross, in July of 1998, provided concrete documents to the KLA about respecting international conventions and that these documents that had been provided by the Red Cross were circulated and respected. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, but I don't know whether it was July. Many humanitarian organisations came to us at that time. It could be July. It could be later. There were some small leaflets in Albanian, and their main points were how to deal with war prisoners. These were little leaflets or very small manuals, and we distributed those in many places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's your best memory of when it was? Jakup Krasniqi said it was in July. What's your best memory when those leaflets were distributed?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when OSCE came. After the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement, many organisations came to us, and I think they had a lot of these booklets of leaflets that they brought to us. In the beginning, their intention was for us to distribute them to our soldiers, but when OSCE came there were more of them, of these leaflets. The Red Cross also, they had their own leaflets that they gave us to distribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, Mr. Limaj, your testimony is that it was later. Your testimony is that the dates were later, that it was October when this happened. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was in July and September, October when these organisations came. But in the beginning, there were very few of them -- of those leaflets, in July. I personally had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you were, during the war, a fanatic for discipline and order, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried my best to keep order and discipline. When I knew what my mandate was, what my duties were, I tried to be a principled person and tried to keep order. I tried to do my best. When I had things clear in my mind, what I was told clearly what my duties were, I tried to abide by the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't just try to abide by them, you were a fanatic for order and discipline; right? You know why I'm using those words, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't understand why you're using this word "fanatic." What I said is that I tried to keep order and discipline as far as I could, as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play a short clip for you from -- it's from Exhibit P35, which is a documentary that was made after your arrest. It's about you, and the clip is -- appears to be from March of 1999, and it's you speaking to some KLA soldiers. And if you could just watch carefully, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I said that was -- appeared to be from March, but -- exactly. It says May 1999 on the transcript. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in May. Yes, I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that -- I take it that that's -- the attitude that you expressed there to the soldiers was your attitude -- that wasn't something new. That was your attitude throughout the war. Right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, Mr. Prosecutor, all my life, both civil life and life in the army, show my best intentions. Here we had volunteers, soldiers who had come as volunteers from various western countries. Here in this film it was taken in Albania, on the border with Albania. These are people who had lived in a different environment and they had come to join the army. This was the first speech I gave to them. I had to tell them these things because they had no idea what they were getting into. So this was before a battle. This was a battle. You might have heard about an operation, Shigheta, an arrow in English. These are young men from America, the Atlantic Battalion. There were people from other western countries. So they had to be prepared for the battle. I didn't want them to flee. Some of them had radios or tape recorders with themselves. I told them to leave them aside. They had entered another life now and they had to be prepared. And that's why I spoke to them the way I did. I tried my best to keep order. But in May it was different. It was different in 1999. It was not like in 1998. Now, here, I was speaking to these soldiers as Deputy Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand that things changed from 1998 to 1999. What I was talking about was your attitude about order and discipline. That didn't change, did it? That was the same in 1999 as it was in 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1998, it was different. We started then with friends and nephews and relatives, and we formed an army. These people in the film, they had come from America. It was much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I don't think you listened to my question, and it may be because you thought I was asking something different or you're listening to some of the English, I'm not sure. But please listen carefully to the question. I understand that things changed from 1998 to 1999 with the KLA, but what I'm putting to you did not change was your attitude about discipline and order. Your attitude about it. Your personal attitude about it was the same in 1999 as it was in 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to answer you, but I don't think you like my answer. That's why you say I'm not answering your question. I said of course in 1998 it was desirable to have discipline among the soldiers, but we did not have the experience. We did not know how to enforce discipline. It's different when you speak about something that is desirable and something that is enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that precise point and go back to 1998, to the time period that we're interested in, May, June and July of 1998. During that time period if soldiers misbehaved in the KLA, they could have their weapons taken away, they could have their uniforms taken away, and they could be expelled from the KLA; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to explain. I will give an example of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But before you explain, the answer to that question is yes; right? Those things could --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say yes. I have to explain. Please allow me to explain the experiences as they were at that time. If you allow me, I will explain how things were with my unit. I can't say yes or no. I have to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But please explain, but if while you're explaining you could answer the question I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried from the beginning to answer your questions as best as I can because it's in my interest. During these months that you mentioned, if the soldier came with his own weapon and if they misbehaved, the only thing that we could tell him was, "Go away." We couldn't take his weapon away. But if the soldier came without a weapon and I gave him a weapon, then he did something wrong, I could take his weapon and tell him to go home. He probably went to the other unit and stayed there. If I took away his weapon, he could go to the next unit and stay there or to another place where there was fighting and got a weapon there. So these were our possibilities at that time. The uniform. There was no way. It never happened in Kosovo at the time. We -- you couldn't tell this person, "You can't stay in my unit." If you did tell them, they would go to the next unit or another unit in another village, because we could not communicate with the other unit and tell them that we recommended not take this person as a soldier. There was no communication. So these were the two things that we could do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There may have been an error in the translation or you misspoke. Just to be clear, you could tell a person that they can't -- that person couldn't stay in your unit but your testimony is the person could go to another unit; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean that he didn't ask us about that, he just went there. He went there on his own, not that I told him to go to the next unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. But you could tell somebody that he couldn't be in your unit any more. That was one thing that you could do. That's your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to my unit. I'm speaking about my unit. If the soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about my unit. At that time, it could be that one said, "You cannot stay here. Go away." He probably didn't listen to us at all, but practically the person -- the person could choose whether to stay and disregard what I said or leave, whatever he did -- whatever he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're saying that if the -- if a soldier was told by the unit commander to go away that he could decide to stay? He could just stay?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he could have said no. That's what I'm saying. But in fact in my unit, if I told a person to leave, then he had to leave. He could have said no, but you could see that person in the next unit somewhere else, I mean, immediately. And in fact, his answer could be, "You cannot stop me from fighting elsewhere. I can fight wherever I want."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But in fact he would have left your unit if he had been told to leave. In fact, he would have left; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in July of 1998, in -- before the offensive, do you recall taking Fadil Kastrati's weapon away from him because he had a dispute from somebody in his village? Do you recall doing that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, Mr. Prosecutor, but I'd like to explain how it was because you made a very big deal of this and I'd like to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me first just -- let me just ask the questions and I'll give you an opportunity to explain if it's necessary; okay? So you recall doing it. You recall taking his weapon away; correct? In July before the offensive.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the case. Not that I took away his weapon, but I can remember the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it took place -- the case that you remember, it took place in July before the offensive; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was before the offensive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It occurred in Blinaje?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It occurred in Blinaje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fadil Kastrati had a dispute with somebody in his village in Blinaje; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything further about it. But I'd like to explain how I went to Blinaje, how it came up to that point, how I met him. I don't know how to respond to you because I don't know what Fadil Kastrati did, but I'd like the opportunity to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I give that you opportunity, let me just ask one more question. Shukri Buja was the commander in Blinaje at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Shukri Buja at that time was zone commander. You know very well that at the time Shukri Buja was the zone command, not a commander in Blinaje. He told you in his first interview. He told you here that. He was zone commander at the time. I told you a hundred times, Mr. Prosecutor. I think you know very well, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm trying to tell you everything I know, but you're trying by all means to build something that cannot be built. Please allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, why don't you explain to the Court how it was you took the weapon away from Fadil Kastrati.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, sometime in July -- Blinaje is a national park and I think it was the only park in Kosovo. There was no other park with various animals in Kosovo at the time. Because UCK was there at the time -- because Jakup was in Kroimire. I met Jakup, and from that Shukri told me, "Will you come with me to Blinaje to see the park?" I went with Shukri to Blinaje to see the park. There were a couple of government buildings there, former government buildings. There were some soldiers staying there. Fadil's brother used to be LDK representative for the village. Fadil's brother was a commander in Blinaje at the time, not Shukri Buja, and he told Shukri -- he told Shukri, "Take Fadil's weapon away because he's going to be killed. They are going to have a shoot-out with his neighbour because they had this dispute. Take my brother's weapon away because he's not listening to me." And Shukri said, "Well, I cannot do that because it is his weapon." So his brother told me, "You're somebody he doesn't know, we don't know. Please don't let my brother get into a blood feud. Take his weapon away." So I told him, "You have to give up your weapon because this is the order from above. We shouldn't do these things in a war. We need to cooperate with civilians and not ill-treat them." Now, you analyse it the way you want, but this is how it happened. There was a danger that blood feud would arise from this. Sofa deal was not listening to his brother, and because they pleaded with me to speak to him, that's why I spoke to Fadil. You try to make a big deal out of it, but this is the truth. While about Shukri Buja being a commander in Blinaje, forget it. He never was a command near Blinaje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony was it was just a coincidence. You were going to the park in Blinaje and you were there that day and they asked you -- just because you happened to be there, by coincidence, they asked you to take the weapon away from Fadil Kastrati. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is the only truth. There is no other truth. No other truth, Mr. Prosecutor. You can interpret it the way you want, but I'm telling you the way it happened. I don't know how Fadil perceived it because of the way I spoke to him. Blini was his brother's pseudonym. I know that he was head of LDK himself, so Blini and myself and Shukri told him that. And it was just a coincidence, yes. You give it the weight you want, Your Honours, but this was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the map that the witness marked, could that be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecution Exhibit P247.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour may recall that you kindly allowed an opportunity at the end of cross-examination but before re-examination in the light of material that had not been previously disclosed for me to have time to speak to Mr. Limaj. We have only spoken to him about matters up to now, about the toothache and so on. So if we may take that opportunity. I have a suggestion. I hope it's acceptable. The break comes up very shortly I think, 20 past the hour if we could resume as it would have been after the break at twenty to, that affords us plenty of time to deal with -- it's a book, if you recall and as I understood in evidence he marked it up. I don't know what the markings are and I may need a bit Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of time to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because there is a delegation which must be met by members of the Chamber during this break, we would not be able to resume until ten minutes to the hour. Is that time enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we break now and resume at ten minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I take Your Honours for the time and make clear that in fact having as it were examined the book issue, Mr. Limaj doesn't wish to add anything to the matters he's already said on that score. So I'm not going back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, just a few matters in re-examination, and one of them, the prime one I want to deal with is this question of zones and, I'm afraid, maps again. I wonder if you could have for these purposes the map you originally marked up with the operational zones and the brigade, which was -- or is, DL7. I've asked for it to be made available. And then alongside that I'd like you to have, please, P1, map 10. Mr. Limaj, if you would bear with me. It's going to be, with permission, slightly longer question than usual from me, and I want to do it to illustrate the selection that I objected to that was going on in the cross-examination, the way matters were put to you, and I'm going to use this as an illustration. The suggestion that was put to you about what you were saying vis-a-vis the zones, particularly in relation to that map that you have in front of you, the one you marked up, and it's Monday, May the 23rd, page 6181, line 4, the suggestion put clearly to you was that you were redrawing, effectively, the zones in order to try and put the Lapusnik village outside of the Pashtrik zone and to put it into Sylejman Selimi's zone. Now, that was the suggestion. And before I ask you to elaborate a little bit more on this, I want to put to you, which was not put to you, what the evidence has been about this from some key witnesses, if you remember it. Mr. Selimi himself was questioned by Mr. Nicholls on Monday the 17th of January, 2005, page 2089, about the map 10, P1, that you have there. That's the other one, the Prosecution map, where Drenica is -- the zone is marked in red as is the village of Lapusnik. And he was asked to look at that map with regard to the zones. The question he was asked was this: "Looking at the Drenica zone," that's on map 10, "is that the area mapped out as the Drenica zone? Is that roughly accurate for the date concerned?" And he said this at line 13: "Yes. More or less it's clear here. There are many villages that are not marked here but more or less this is the zone, yes." And we can see where Lapusnik is marked on map 10. That's one witness. Jakup Krasniqi on Tuesday the 15th of February of this year, page 3474, line 8 onwards was asked by me about the same topic. "I want to ask you about Lapusnik in particular. You already indicated that Lapusnik was in the municipality of Gllogovc which itself was in Drenica. So is it your evidence that Lapusnik came within the zone that in fact was most organised during April to August, namely Drenica?" Answer: "Yes." And finally this witness, Shukri Buja, on Thursday the 10th of March, 2005, at page 4099, also asked by me, line 6, as to the position of Lapusnik in the subzone of Drenica, and he answered: "I cannot confirm it officially, but I do know that when we were appointed commanders of subzones it was done on the basis of villages of the municipalities. And to my recollection Lapusnik," and he gives a number of other villages, "which were part of the former Gllogovc commune, as it was called, in Drenica." Now, those are the three witnesses who were dealing with this. And I want to ask you again given that suggestion put to you in the clearest terms that you, as opposed to others, were manipulating the boundaries, and the question simply is this: Have you manipulated boundaries in order to push Lapusnik into somebody else's zone?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already stated this in the beginning, and I will repeat it. The idea of subzones or zones for their establishment based itself on the territory that the municipalities comprised. This existed as an idea in March or April, and this continued up to August. When the reorganisation took part in August, it was then when the zone territories were redefined. Some became smaller, some became larger depending on the situation in the terrain. This is my answer. But the idea was that in the beginning, to base the territory of the zones according to the territory of municipalities. And after August, the definition was made according to the circumstances in the terrain. Boundaries were changed, zones were changed, and units were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to focus on Lapusnik. In which zone did Lapusnik fall at the beginning of this period?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even here I will stress again that the idea of forming the zone is based on municipalities. Lapusnik is in Drenoc municipality. That was the idea of organising at that time, and this was until August. After August, this principle was abandoned and the zones were organised according to military ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the military ideas in fact you have put on your version of map 6, which is DL7. I think you have it there. There are three different colours on there, and just to recapitulate on that Brigade 121, just to take it in stages, when was the brigade first considered as a concept?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a concept, 121st Brigade was envisaged to be as such, but later on as time passed we defined the borderline. I here refer to the part -- Malisheve part, because the offensive prevented us from any further organisation. We were totally destroyed. We had to reconstruct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And the beginning of the reconstruction started when, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I described it, Your Honours, we began reconstructing it immediately after the entrance of Serb forces in Klecke and as the territory became smaller. The main purpose was not the reconstruction, but our priority was to build up a defence line for the population. And as I said, in September or October the brigade was of a satisfactory level, and in mid-November we reached a desirable level and were better in comparison with other brigades. I did not have the problem of my soldiers deserting the army. They all remained within the ranks until the end was over, and this helped in the reconstruction of the brigade. The majority of my soldiers had their families in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: A final question on this series of topics, related topics. On the analysis that you have just described, when did Lapusnik first become effectively within the jurisdiction of the 121st or the 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the 121 Brigade was formed, when its boundaries were defined as were the boundaries of the Pashtrik zone, in fact Lapusnik never belonged to the jurisdiction of 121 Brigade. However, when it was decided the main road to be a border of the zone, the part on this side of the Berisha Mountains belonged to 121 Brigade. However, most of Lapusnik continued to remain part of Drenica zone. I want to say that we never, ever controlled that territory, to the end of the war, because the Serb forces were constantly there. The war was no longer waged at Lapusnik. The war was waged in Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want you to take, please, another map, because you were asked about routes into Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And in fact it's the DL4, the ordinance or comparative ordinance survey map, pre-war. If that's available, please. Sorry. DL4. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: There's only one question. If you'd just take it for a moment, because it may not take a lot of time. The question relates to this map, of which we have copies. This arises out of the questioning about other ways into Lapusnik. Do you remember being asked those questions by Mr. Whiting? And you have already described how you might go through the Lapusnik area on your way north and how you might stop off to see people and so on. Does the map show any other road or track from Klecka into Lapusnik that you can see?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You cannot see clearly any other track except for the one that I described. Your Honours, I don't know whether this is on your monitors, but you can see for yourselves how the terrain is here. Here is Lapusnik, Your Honours. If you want me, I can mark the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Lapusnik. Klecke is already marked, Your Honours. Klecke is the one here. This is Klecke. And as you can see, there's no other track except for the one that I described, the one that I described which was used to go from Klecke to Lapusnik or to Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one more question. I'm afraid it's all to do with maps, but you mentioned it today, and that is in relation to the detention of the Serbian journalists. You wanted to point out where that was because it was on the boundary, you indicated, or at least borders with the Serb troops at that point. And I think, if fact, the place you mentioned is on --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resinovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. It isn't on that large scale map but it's on DL7 which you marked up. If you could put that back on the monitor. And in a different colour yet again if there is one, just circle the place where the Serb journalists were detained.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I mentioned Magure, this here is Magure and here you see the brigade boundary and this area here was under Serb control. They entered this track here and came up to here, to this village here, which is Resinovc. Resinovc and Shale are adjoined to each other, attached. This is the place where they were held. Here we had a brigade, a unit which controlled the entrances to the territory. And on this part here the Serb forces were deployed. And I will circle Magure as well, as the place from where they entered the brigade territory, and the soldiers then stopped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions about maps. One final question to you. You will recall today that you were asked to look at a clip - I'm not asking for it to be shown again - a clip, P35, which relates to events in May 1999 when you were addressing potential recruits to the Atlantic Battalion, and you stressed, and it was pointed out to you you were stressing the need for order and discipline. And the question I want to ask you is: At that dangerous and before, for that matter, what did the KLA mean to you as a soldier who had been fighting for at least a year by then?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on that occasion, I had nothing else to say to those young men. That was the only way, to address them orally. This was the first time for them there to join the war, and we just wanted us to be organised and to have less casualties, and that's why I addressed them, to avoid things that can be expected from young people. They were people, young people from the west, and we had experienced many things in Kosova. We had lost many young men because of lack of discipline. Forty-two members of ours were killed on the Kosova-Albanian border because of the discipline, and someone was responsible for that. We had already experienced the reality inside Kosova. The KLA meant -- being a member meant not only to have the will and the zeal to fight but also to protect the human potential, because we were not aware about the figures, how many people were still left in Kosova. At that time, we didn't even know whether our own families were still alive inside Kosova. What personally I felt as a KLA member, I was very satisfied for being a promoter of positive changes not only in my own country. The NATO decision brought about changes not only for the democracy in Kosova but in the region as well. It brought democratic changes in Serbia itself. The democratic class, the citizens who were interested in democracy, they in the end forced that criminal regime to withdraw. We have evidence when the democratic class was ready to fight Milosevic regime if he decided not to step down from power. These were positive changes not only in Kosova. Even if you turned to Bosnia, Croatia, we are facing a totally different situation from the one that was in Kosova before the entrance of NATO troops. Myself as a simple citizen, I found myself that I was right. I woke up and the right side, because with the help of NATO, we managed to bring freedom and to bring those displaced persons back to Kosova. After the confusing situation in Kosova, we tried to find a solution. In other words, as a member of the KLA, I hoped that we will achieve freedom, and I am satisfied that this was the opinion of the international community as well. And what is most important for me is that we were hand-in-hand with western democracies. Now, as to our potential, what was our potential, what was our knowledge, that is something to be discussed, but to what we had, to that knowledge that we had, we did our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no other questions. I pause in case Your Honours do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mansfield. Thank you, Mr. Limaj. You now may return to your position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were just looking at the hour, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's a very intriguing invitation. However, I wonder if I might just -- there are rather obvious reasons -- I would just like to start the next witness, but I might stop at twenty to if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Rexhep Selimi. He's just outside the door. Rexhep Selimi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is coming, could I mention to counsel that there has been filed a Defence motion concerning disclosure in respect of which a considerably shortened time for response by the Prosecution has been fixed by the Chamber, and because of that it should be possible to give consideration to that motion in the course of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- read allowed the affirmation that is on the card handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, I'm over here representing Mr. Limaj, as you know, and may I first tender an apology that you've had to wait rather a long time before being called. I will speak slowly so that my questions can be translated, and if you can adopt the same habit of waiting for the translation, then the interpreters will be happier. If I may lead you on some background matters first of all. Your name is Rexhep Selimi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And you were born on the 15th of March, 1971, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And during the conflict 1998 to 1999, you became a member or were a member of the General Staff at that time but in different positions.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: However, I want to deal with a time before the war and Fatmir Limaj in particular. Can you recall now when you first met Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: It should be in 1991 or 1992. It was in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And where? Where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What were you doing? What were you doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: I was studying at Pristina University. I was a student.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And were you studying the same subjects as Fatmir or something else?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: No. I was studying Albanian language and literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And at any time whilst you were at the university did there come a time when you started living with him in the same accommodation?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And roughly when was that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: It could be during the years I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm not going to trouble you with precise dates. It's some time ago. But I want to move to the KLA. At that time when you were at university, did you become interested in the KLA yourself?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And again, can you give us a rough idea which year that might have been that you became interested?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: In the beginning, I began to show interest in this, in how I can find myself in an organisation with which I would contribute to my country. As for KLA, I showed my interest first in 1993, and I achieved it in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what do you mean by achieving it in 1994?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: We achieved to have an organisation called Kosovo Liberation Army in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Do you regard yourself as a founding member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Fortunately, I was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And at that time, as far as you are concerned, what were the objectives of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: The freedom of Kosova, its liberation with the possible means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what means were being contemplated at that time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Up to that time, the Albanians of Kosova have tried different means, political means and other forms of organisation and gatherings in different political organisations, but we were running out of these means, and to our wish or -- not to our wish, this was the only way for the people of Kosova to engage in order to achieve the freedom of its country and people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to for a moment just ask you about something else at this period, that is the period that you were at university, the same university as Fatmir Limaj. Do you recall an initiative which had as its object the reconciliation of people who might be concerned in blood feuds?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you just please collaborate on what to was as you understood it in those years.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: In those years, this was a great movement. At that time it was called national movement for reconciliation of people who might been concerned in blood feuds. And this initiative taken by certain young men, it was some students, in fact, and with the support of certain intellectuals and the leadership of this initiative by a person, well-known person as Anton Ceta, this initiative expanded and succeeded in reconciliating many families involved in blood feud.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to move on. You talked about the KLA and the founding of it in 1994, and I want to move to 1997. So it's three years later. Were you aware that Fatmir had to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: I didn't have accurate knowledge as to where Fatmir was in 1997, and there was no way how I could, because I was in such circumstances that I couldn't know. After his return from Switzerland, I realised that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you just indicate why in 1997 you couldn't know because of your circumstances? Could you just explain to the Tribunal what you mean by that, please?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: I'll try. At the end of 1996, I had to flee the country because I was persecuted by the Serbian police. I said I had to flee from Pristina and to find a shelter in Prekaz because I was obliged under the circumstances. Therefore, I was unable to follow up developments either in Pristina or somewhere else. Likewise, in January 1997, wanting to arrest and liquidate the KLA members, Serbia organised a large-scale campaign of arrests in Kosova. Among the arrested persons was my brother and many friends of mine, and among the wanted persons I found out that Fatmir Limaj was one of them. So since I was not in Pristina and was not a member of the public life and because of the circumstances created for Fatmir, too, it was impossible for me to know his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, we know that he returned, and there's no issue about this, in 1998 in the spring. But before reaching that, and I'm afraid we won't reach it today but on Monday, just this: What was the KLA doing in 1996, 1997 before Fatmir returned in March 1998? What was it doing in those years?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: During the entire period of the growth of the KLA but especially during this phase, the KLA tried to organise itself better, to have more people joining it, to spread among more places, and especially after the blow, I am using the word "blow" or the attack by the Serbian forces in the beginning of 1997, the entire activity of us who had remained was to reorganise. So I can say that exclusively we dealt only with the reorganisation of that modest structure we had. So in addition to being arrested three of our friends were killed. Zahir Bajaziti, Zenel Lahu [phoen] and Eden [phoen] Hoxha and some others were arrested. This happened at the end of January 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry it's a short day today for you, but at least a start. But my last question is this: During that time that you discussed we have just discussed, was there in existence something called the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: At this time there was in existence an organisation called Central Staff composed of people who had formed it. Among them was myself. It was called Central Staff, not on account of its functioning and organisation but because it was a sort of centre for people to meet, people coming from various regions and working for the same objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And was that Central Staff located in one place or in different places?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI
utterances.text: It depended on the circumstances and situations, but mainly it held its meetings in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time, as I promised. So maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Unfortunately, Mr. Selimi, as you understand we must finish today. Another trial continues after the break, and we resume on Monday at 2.15. So I must ask you to return then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
